title: Algebra Lab — Build a Finite Field Library

questions.question: Which property turns Z/pZ into a field when p is prime?
options: Every nonzero residue has a multiplicative inverse modulo p
Every residue has additive order exactly equal to p always
Every multiplication avoids wraparound, so it behaves like integers
Every element is a generator of the multiplicative group automatically
questions.explanation: Prime p implies gcd(a, p) = 1 for every 1 ≤ a < p, so Extended Euclid yields an inverse for every nonzero residue.

questions.question: In GF(p^m) constructed as F_p[x]/(f(x)), what does irreducibility of f(x) ensure?
options: The quotient has no zero divisors, so every nonzero element is invertible
The quotient has exactly p elements, so it matches the base field size
The quotient has characteristic m, so it matches the polynomial degree
The quotient has no roots in any field, so division is never needed
questions.explanation: Irreducible f(x) makes the quotient a field (an integral domain of the right size), so all nonzero classes have inverses.

questions.question: Why should your element type reject adding values from different finite fields?
options: Because cancellation laws and inverses only make sense inside one field
Because it is always slower to add across fields than within one field
Because finite fields prohibit addition unless p is larger than 2^64
Because the result would overflow Python integers and lose precision
questions.explanation: Field identities are scoped to one structure. Mixing parameters silently turns valid algebra into undefined behavior.

questions.question: Why does an extension-field implementation reduce every product modulo f(x)?
options: To keep representatives at degree < m and enforce the relation f(x) = 0
To make multiplication commutative, which otherwise fails for polynomials
To guarantee every element becomes a primitive generator of the field
To ensure all coefficients stay equal to 0 or 1 regardless of p value
questions.explanation: Reduction modulo f(x) keeps a canonical representative and implements arithmetic in the quotient ring F_p[x]/(f).

questions.question: In AES-style GF(2^8) arithmetic, what is addition of two bytes?
options: Bitwise XOR, because polynomial coefficients add modulo 2
Integer addition mod 256, because bytes are elements of Z/256Z
Bitwise AND, because coefficients multiply when adding polynomials
Bitwise OR, because coefficients are forced to remain in {0,1}
questions.explanation: AES treats bytes as polynomials over F_2, and addition in F_2 is XOR, so polynomial addition is byte-wise XOR.

questions.question: Which method is the right core tool to compute inverses in F_p[x]/(f(x)) from scratch?
options: Extended Euclidean algorithm in F_p[x], run against f(x)
Trial division over integers, run against p until a factor is found
Floating-point Newton iteration, run until the reciprocal converges
Discrete logarithm, run by searching for the exponent that yields one
questions.explanation: If gcd(a(x), f(x)) = 1, extended GCD returns x(x) with a(x)x(x) ≡ 1 (mod f). That x(x) is the inverse.

questions.question: You accidentally construct F_p[x]/(f(x)) with reducible f(x). What is the failure mode?
options: Some nonzero elements become non-invertible because zero divisors appear
All nonzero elements become generators, so inversion becomes ambiguous
The field characteristic changes, so addition no longer matches modulo p
Nothing breaks; reducibility only affects performance, not correctness
questions.explanation: Reducible f(x) yields a ring with zero divisors. Nonzero elements can multiply to zero, so inverses stop existing.

questions.question: Why should production crypto avoid using this course's from-scratch field code?
options: It is not side-channel hardened and is not designed for constant-time safety
It uses modular arithmetic, which is forbidden in modern cryptographic code
It cannot represent extension fields at all, only prime fields GF(p)
It guarantees incorrect results whenever p is prime and m is greater than 1
questions.explanation: Correct math is not enough. Production implementations need constant-time arithmetic, vetted parameters, and security review.
